items.stem: Which term describes shared products, values, media and lifestyles found in many societies across the world?
items.answer: Global culture
items.markingKey: Global culture: shared products, values, media and lifestyles found in many societies across the world. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “homogenisation”, and give one example.
items.answer: The process by which cultures become more similar. Example: the same shopping malls and brands in every city.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the process by which cultures become more similar); 1 mark for a relevant example such as the same shopping malls and brands in every city. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “Americanisation” and “homogenisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Americanisation: the spread of American products, values and culture around the world (e.g. American fast food, films and slang in many countries). Homogenisation: the process by which cultures become more similar (e.g. the same shopping malls and brands in every city).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A survey in Colombo finds that most of the top 20 films last year were made in Hollywood, but the most-streamed music was by local artists. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: global culture offers more choice; people mix global and local elements to create their own identities (hybridity).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In Jakarta, the main shopping street now has the same coffee chains, fast-food outlets and clothing brands as cities across the world, and local cafés have closed. Explain how a neo-Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: rationalised, standardised culture spreads the logic of capitalism into everyday life, creating an iron cage (Ritzer).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A hospital in Colombo introduces strict time targets for each consultation and a scripted checklist for staff to follow with every patient. Compare how postmodernist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: global culture offers more choice; people mix global and local elements to create their own identities (hybridity). Marxism: global culture is driven by TNCs spreading consumerism and capitalist values for profit; local cultures are swamped (Sklair, Schiller).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Freya, a sociology student, is designing a project on the amount of foreign content on national television. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitations: it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it; counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the amount of foreign content on national television but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Daniel is planning a study of the amount of foreign content on national television. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the amount of foreign content on national television but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the domination of other cultures by the values and products of powerful (mainly Western) societies?
items.answer: Cultural imperialism
items.markingKey: Cultural imperialism: the domination of other cultures by the values and products of powerful (mainly Western) societies. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “Americanisation”.
items.answer: The spread of American products, values and culture around the world.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the spread of American products, values and culture around the world. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “culture-ideology of consumerism” and “homogenisation”?
items.answer: Culture-ideology of consumerism: Sklair’s term for the values encouraging people to define themselves through buying goods. Homogenisation: the process by which cultures become more similar.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A content analysis of prime-time television in a country produced the results below. Table: share of prime-time hours on national television (%) | 2000 | 2020. Domestic programmes | 42% | 53%. US programmes | 37% | 23%. Other foreign programmes | 21% | 24%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Domestic programmes change between 2000 and 2020?
items.answer: +11 percentage points
items.markingKey: 53 − 42 = +11 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows a content analysis of prime-time schedules in a country near Santiago. Table: share of prime-time hours on national television (%) | 2000 | 2020. Domestic programmes | 44% | 55%. US programmes | 33% | 25%. Other foreign programmes | 23% | 20%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for US programmes between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that cultural imperialism is declining.
items.answer: (a) (25 − 33) ÷ 33 × 100 = -24.2%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Domestic programmes; the figure fell for US programmes, Other foreign programmes; Domestic programmes had the highest figure for 2020. More content comes from non-US countries. Qualifications: Streaming platforms may not be included; local programmes may copy US formats; ownership of channels may still be foreign. The data also come from content analysis of 3 channels in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (25 − 33) ÷ 33 × 100; 1 mark for -24.2% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which global culture may affect local cultures.
items.answer: Homogenisation and Americanisation; McDonaldisation; consumerism; hybridity and glocalisation; revival of local identities as resistance.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Homogenisation and Americanisation; McDonaldisation; consumerism; hybridity and glocalisation; revival of local identities as resistance. [8]

items.stem: A content analysis of prime-time television in a country produced the results below. Table: share of prime-time hours on national television (%) | 2000 | 2020. Domestic programmes | 43% | 56%. US programmes | 33% | 28%. Other foreign programmes | 24% | 16%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Other foreign programmes between 2000 and 2020. (b) Explain one limitation of using content analysis to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that cultural imperialism is declining.
items.answer: (a) 16 − 24 = -8 percentage points. (b) It shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Domestic programmes; the figure fell for US programmes, Other foreign programmes; Domestic programmes had the highest figure for 2020. Quotas for domestic content. Qualifications: Streaming platforms may not be included; local programmes may copy US formats; ownership of channels may still be foreign. The data also come from content analysis of 3 channels in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 24 and 16; 1 mark for -8 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the mixing of different cultures to create new cultural forms and identities?
items.answer: Hybridity
items.markingKey: Hybridity: the mixing of different cultures to create new cultural forms and identities. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “hybridity”, and give one example.
items.answer: The mixing of different cultures to create new cultural forms and identities. Example: Bhangra music mixing Punjabi folk and Western pop.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the mixing of different cultures to create new cultural forms and identities); 1 mark for a relevant example such as Bhangra music mixing Punjabi folk and Western pop. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “hyphenated identity” and “global identity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Hyphenated identity: an identity combining two cultural or national belongings (e.g. British-Pakistani or Chinese-Canadian). Global identity: a sense of belonging to the world as a whole rather than one nation (e.g. young people describing themselves as “global citizens”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Aisha, whose parents migrated to Kathmandu from another continent, speaks two languages at home, follows K-pop and celebrates both her family’s festivals and local holidays. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identities are fluid and chosen; people mix global and local influences to create hybrid identities (Hall, Pieterse).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A global coffee chain in Riyadh offers drinks made with local spices and designs its cafés to resemble traditional tea houses. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: identity is negotiated in everyday interaction; individuals give their own meanings to cultural mixing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research how global brands adapt their products in different countries.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how global brands adapt their products in different countries but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the adaptation of global products and ideas to fit local cultures?
items.answer: Glocalisation
items.markingKey: Glocalisation: the adaptation of global products and ideas to fit local cultures. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “hyphenated identity”?
items.answer: An identity combining two cultural or national belongings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: an identity combining two cultural or national belongings. [1]

items.stem: Mateo is planning a study of how global brands adapt their products in different countries. Explain one limitation of using content analysis for this research.
items.answer: It shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it.

items.stem: A global coffee chain in Auckland offers drinks made with local spices and designs its cafés to resemble traditional tea houses. Explain how transformationalist and Marxist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Transformationalism: global and local interact: global products are adapted locally, producing glocalisation rather than simple domination (Robertson). Marxism: glocalisation is a marketing strategy by TNCs to increase profits; hybridity still takes place on terms set by global capitalism.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a population that has spread from its original homeland but keeps a shared identity and links to it?
items.answer: Diaspora
items.markingKey: Diaspora: a population that has spread from its original homeland but keeps a shared identity and links to it. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “transnational community”, and give one example.
items.answer: A group that maintains social, economic and political ties across national borders. Example: migrants sending remittances and voting in home elections.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a group that maintains social, economic and political ties across national borders); 1 mark for a relevant example such as migrants sending remittances and voting in home elections. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “push factors” and “remittances”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Push factors: conditions that encourage people to leave their country (e.g. unemployment, conflict or persecution). Remittances: money sent home by migrants to their families (e.g. a nurse abroad sending money monthly to parents).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Members of a community originally from one country now live in Kathmandu and five other cities; they run a shared website, fund a school in their home region and vote in its elections. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: migrants provide cheap, flexible labour for capitalism in richer countries, and migration drains skills from poorer countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Members of a community originally from one country now live in Santiago and five other cities; they run a shared website, fund a school in their home region and vote in its elections. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: migration creates diaspora and hybrid identities; people belong to several places and choose identities (Hall, Cohen).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research patterns of international migration over time.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying patterns of international migration over time but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “feminisation of migration”.
items.answer: The growing share of women among international migrants.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the growing share of women among international migrants. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “transnational community” and “remittances”.
items.answer: Transnational community: a group that maintains social, economic and political ties across national borders. Remittances: money sent home by migrants to their families.

items.stem: A sociologist in Dubai wants to research patterns of international migration over time. Explain one strength of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified.

items.stem: Members of a community originally from one country now live in Cairo and five other cities; they run a shared website, fund a school in their home region and vote in its elections. Compare how Marxist and Marxist feminist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: migrants provide cheap, flexible labour for capitalism in richer countries, and migration drains skills from poorer countries. Marxist feminism: women’s migration for care work creates global care chains in which poor women’s labour is exploited to support richer families (Ehrenreich and Hochschild).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes Ritzer’s term for the spread of the fast-food principles of efficiency, calculability, predictability and control?

items.markingKey: McDonaldisation: Ritzer’s term for the spread of the fast-food principles of efficiency, calculability, predictability and control. [1]

items.stem: Explain Sklair’s argument that TNCs spread a culture-ideology of consumerism, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Sklair argued the transnational capitalist class promotes consumption as the meaning of life. Criticism: Postmodernists argue consumers actively use goods to build identities.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful semi-structured interviews are for studying how young people in Mexico City view global brands.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth. Limitations: samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited; follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how young people in Mexico City view global brands but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying how global brands adapt their products in different countries.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how global brands adapt their products in different countries but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).

items.stem: Briefly explain Ehrenreich and Hochschild’s view that women from poorer countries migrate to provide care work in richer countries, creating global care chains.

items.stem: A sociologist in Mexico City wants to research the experiences of migrant care workers. Explain two strengths of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: 1. Participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally. 2. They take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the experiences of migrant care workers. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful covert participant observation is for studying the experiences of migrant care workers.
items.answer: Strengths: it may be the only way to study a group that hides its activities from outsiders; it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity. Limitations: secretly recording sensitive behaviour without consent raises serious ethical problems of deception and harm; note-taking is difficult, so data depends on memory and may be inaccurate. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of migrant care workers but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research the amount of foreign content on national television.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the amount of foreign content on national television but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: The table shows a content analysis of prime-time schedules in a country near Cape Town. Table: share of prime-time hours on national television (%) | 2000 | 2020. Domestic programmes | 40% | 49%. US programmes | 40% | 35%. Other foreign programmes | 20% | 16%. (a) Calculate the gap between US programmes and Other foreign programmes in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that cultural imperialism is declining.
items.answer: (a) 2000: 20 percentage points; 2020: 19 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Domestic programmes; the figure fell for US programmes, Other foreign programmes; Domestic programmes had the highest figure for 2020. Local producers have grown and audiences prefer local programmes. Qualifications: Streaming platforms may not be included; local programmes may copy US formats; ownership of channels may still be foreign. The data also come from content analysis of 3 channels in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (20 and 19); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes a sense of belonging to the world as a whole rather than one nation?
items.answer: Global identity
items.markingKey: Global identity: a sense of belonging to the world as a whole rather than one nation. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “hybridity”.
items.answer: The mixing of different cultures to create new cultural forms and identities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the mixing of different cultures to create new cultural forms and identities. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which globalisation may create hybrid identities.
items.answer: Migration brings cultures together and second generations mix them; global media let people choose from many cultures; consumption of global goods combined with local traditions; online communities across borders.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: Priya surveyed 450 young people in Manila about their identities. The results are below. Table: how young people describe their identity (%) | Parents born in the country | Parents born abroad. National identity only | 59% | 37%. Mixed or hyphenated identity | 20% | 50%. Global citizen | 21% | 13%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Parents born in the country and Parents born abroad for Global citizen (Parents born abroad minus Parents born in the country)?
items.answer: -8 percentage points
items.markingKey: 13 − 21 = -8 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Chloe, whose parents migrated to Cairo from another continent, speaks two languages at home, follows K-pop and celebrates both her family’s festivals and local holidays. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: glocalisation is a marketing strategy by TNCs to increase profits; hybridity still takes place on terms set by global capitalism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using content analysis to research how global brands adapt their products in different countries.
items.answer: Strengths: it is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain; quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitations: counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context; coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how global brands adapt their products in different countries but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a group that maintains social, economic and political ties across national borders?
items.answer: Transnational community
items.markingKey: Transnational community: a group that maintains social, economic and political ties across national borders. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Remittances flow from poorer countries to richer countries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Remittances are mainly sent by migrants in richer countries back to families in poorer countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Ehrenreich and Hochschild’s argument that women from poorer countries migrate to provide care work in richer countries, creating global care chains, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: They argued care and emotional labour are transferred from poor to rich countries, leaving gaps in migrants’ own families. Criticism: Migrants may gain independence and income through migration.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxist feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows official data on remittances received by three countries. Table: remittances received as a percentage of GDP | 2010 | 2022. Country A | 10% | 15%. Country B | 16% | 19%. Country C | 5% | 6%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Country B change between 2010 and 2022?
items.answer: +3 percentage points
items.markingKey: 19 − 16 = +3 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Chloe works as a nurse in a hospital in Lagos, sends half her wages to her parents abroad each month and uses video calls to help raise her children, who live with their grandmother. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: migrants provide cheap, flexible labour for capitalism in richer countries, and migration drains skills from poorer countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: World Bank figures on remittances received by three countries are shown below. Table: remittances received as a percentage of GDP | 2010 | 2022. Country A | 5% | 8%. Country B | 21% | 23%. Country C | 4% | 6%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Country B between 2010 and 2022. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that migration benefits sending countries.
items.answer: (a) 23 − 21 = +2 percentage points. (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country B had the highest figure for 2022. Economic problems at home push more people to migrate. Qualifications: Remittances do not show the social costs of separated families or the loss of skilled workers (brain drain); informal transfers are not counted. The data also come from official statistics of 3 countries in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 21 and 23; 1 mark for +2 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]
